thesis: Nonliteral expression, semantic equivalence, function and market substitution must be analyzed separately across the AI supply chain.
role: Apply the core distinction to books, authorship and lawful economic harm.

ideas.statement: Lexical, expressive, semantic, functional and commercial equivalence differ; distinctive scenarios and arrangements may survive paraphrase while ideas remain free.
Rights, attribution and factual accuracy need separate reviews; source dependence and copied errors matter as evidence without creating rights in facts.
Acquisition, training, retrieval, prompting, rewriting and publication are distinct acts; lawful input does not authorize every output and independent wording does not cure unlawful acquisition.
Human expressive contribution requires evidence rather than prompt counts; provider ownership terms cannot create absent copyright or remove third-party rights.
Lawful substitutes can harm revenue without infringement; verified services and collective support address sustainability separately from enforcement.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: Translation changes almost every word while remaining an adaptation; an independent treatment of a scientific principle can retain utility without expression.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Memorization evidence concerns studied models; Bartz settlement is not universal training precedent; economic figures and substitution scenarios are illustrative.

audit.notes: Complete batch read; headings and navigation excluded from idea ranking.
